name: Hatam
confidence_why: No usable statement on word stress located.

tone_statements.citation: Reesink, Ger P. 2002. The eastern Bird's Head languages compared. In Ger P. Reesink (ed.), Languages of the eastern Bird's Head, 1-44. Pacific Linguistics 524. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, Australian National University.
tone_statements.quote: Mpur clearly has phonemic tone, M eyah and Sougb a pitch-accent system. Hatam and Mansim do not have a tonal distinction, which they may well have had in the past (the number of homophones in Hatam is considerable), but Hatam does have a very pronounced iambic stress pattern over the utterance as a whole, defying attempts to determine a pattern of word stress.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: The exclusion (phrasal iambic metre, no word-level stress; StressTyp2's second-syllable coding rejected) rests on the best available source, Reesink's 1999 reference grammar, whose dedicated metrical-stress section (pp.32-39) states exactly this and is held and verified verbatim at p.32 and p.39. Donohue 1997, downloaded now, is silent on stress placement and does not disturb the classification. Only bookkeeping is suggested: populate quote/cite/loc/grade from the copy consulted (Reesink 1999:32, section 2.10; grade page-read) instead of leaving them empty with the quotation only in the contra note, and repair the truncated second contra sentence. no reclassification.

sources.citation: Donohue, Mark. 1997. Hatam phonology and grammatical notes. In Andrew Pawley (ed.), Papers in Papuan linguistics No. 3, 37-57. Pacific Linguistics A-87. Canberra: ANU.
sources.quote: No word-stress rule is stated. Stress is invoked only as a diagnostic for epenthetic vs phonemic vowels: 'The stress is noticeably stronger on words containing [ɛ], [a] or [ɔ] than [i] or [u]' (p.44); transcriptions such as /pketa/ [pə'gɛda] show stress never on the epenthetic schwa, consistent with Reesink's 'weak syllable never stressed'.
sources.locator: section 2.4, p.44 (only stress mention); sections 2.1-2.5 contain no stress-placement rule
sources.note: Only other published phonology of Hatam; checked for an independent stress statement (none; silent).

Hatam and Mansim do not have a tonal distinction, which they may well have had in the past (the number of homophones in Hatam is considerable), but Hatam does have a very pronounced iambic stress pattern over the utterance as a whole, defying attempts to determine a pattern of word stress.
sources.note: States that Mpur has phonemic tone and Meyah/Sougb a pitch accent system, but Hatam and Mansim have no tonal distinction (possibly lost; many homophones in Hatam); Hatam instead has a pronounced utterance-level iambic stress pattern with no determinable word stress. Also (p.24, sec.6) cites Gravelle p.c. on a Meyah high/low tone minimal pair.

tone.quote: Clearly, more research is required to ascertain the exact scope of geminates in Hatam, or whether perhaps pitch on the following vowel is the distinctive feature. [...] A preliminary conclusion would be, then, that Hatam fonns a iambic metrum based on length: short-long. In case of syllables of roughly equal length, the peak is phonetically realised by intensity or pitch. [...] I hope to have at least indicated that Hatam is characterised by a clear iambic metre which has full clauses or utterances as its domain, and not some kind of limited word stress.
tone.locator: p. 15 (sec. 2.2 Geminates), p. 35 and p. 39 (sec. 2.10 Metrical stress)
